title: A $10 Chip That Could Put a Medical Lab on Your Wrist
summary:
Imagine checking your blood sugar without a needle, using a sensor on your wrist. Researchers at the University of Cambridge and a start-up called GlitterinTech have built a light-reading chip that could one day make that possible. It costs just $10.

The chip is an optical spectrometer, a tool that studies light to figure out what a substance is made of. Spectrometers are essential in medicine, factories, food testing and environmental research, but shrinking them usually means giving up accuracy. This one is only a few centimeters across, yet the team says its precision rivals much bigger laboratory machines.

The secret is mathematics. The device, called a convolutional spectrometer, analyzes light using a rule called the convolution theorem, performing the math directly on the light itself instead of relying on heavy computer calculations afterward. It works across a range of near-infrared light and finishes a measurement in less than a second.

In tests, the chip correctly identified plastics, medicines, coffee, flour and tea every time. It also measured human health markers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate and blood glucose, under conditions designed to mimic the body. In one demonstration, it tracked one person's blood glucose without needles over an extended period. The researchers caution that much more testing is needed before it could become a real medical product.

'The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra,' said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study.

The chip also kept working from -20°C to 80°C, a range that could suit wearables, factories and outdoor sensors. Professor Qixiang Cheng, who led the project, said what stands out is that the packaged system works reliably in real-world conditions, not just in the lab.
why_it_matters: A cheap, accurate chip could move health checks and material testing out of big laboratories and into wearables, factories and outdoor sensors. That could make useful measurements faster and available in many more places.

background_read: A spectrometer studies light that passes through or bounces off a substance to work out what that substance is made of.
Doctors and scientists use such tools to check health markers, food, medicines and materials, but large laboratory machines are hard to carry around.
Making a spectrometer small, cheap and accurate could let sensors be worn on the body or used in factories and outdoors.
